c: Start with a water tank

Picture a tank on a tower with a pipe running down to a tap. The height of the tank sets how hard the water pushes. The width of the pipe sets how easily it flows. The stream coming out of the tap is the result of those two things together. Electricity behaves closely enough like this that engineers still use the picture. Voltage is the push. Resistance is how narrow the pipe is. Current is the flow that results. Nearly every question you will ask about a circuit is one of these three, hiding behind a part number or a symptom.
Voltage is a difference, not a place

Voltage, measured in volts, is the push between two points. It is always between two points, which is why a multimeter has two probes. A 9 volt battery does not have 9 volts in it. It has 9 volts across it, from one terminal to the other. A bird sits on a power line unharmed because both feet are at the same voltage, so nothing pushes current through the bird. When someone says a point in a circuit is at 5 volts, they mean 5 volts compared with ground, the point everyone agreed to call zero.
Current is what actually moves

Current, measured in amperes or amps, is how much charge passes a point each second. It is the thing that does the work and the thing that does the damage. An LED glows at about 0.02 amps, written 20 milliamps. A phone charger delivers 1 to 3 amps. A car starter motor pulls several hundred for a few seconds. Current only flows around a complete loop, out of the source, through the parts and back again. Break the loop anywhere and it stops everywhere at once, which is all a switch really does.
Resistance sets the price of flow

Resistance, measured in ohms, is how hard a material fights current. Copper wire fights very little, so a metre of hookup wire is a small fraction of an ohm. Rubber, glass and dry air fight so hard that almost nothing gets through. In between sit resistors, parts built to have a known value such as 220 or 10,000 ohms. Designers use them like valves, choosing how much current each branch of a circuit is allowed. Resistance turns electrical energy into heat, which is useful in a toaster and a nuisance nearly everywhere else.
How the three lock together

The three quantities are tied by one rule. For a given resistance, more voltage pushes more current. For a given voltage, more resistance allows less current. Put 9 volts across 450 ohms and 0.02 amps flows. Double the voltage and the current doubles. Double the resistance and the current halves. You never get to pick all three. Choose two and the circuit decides the third for you. That is why a part rated for 5 volts dies on 12: the higher push forces more current through it than it was built to carry.
Units and the prefixes you will meet

Electronics spans enormous ranges, so the units come with prefixes. Milli means a thousandth, micro a millionth. Kilo means a thousand, mega a million. A sensor might draw 50 microamps while the motor beside it draws 2 amps, forty thousand times more. A pull-up resistor might be 10 kilohms and a current sense resistor 10 milliohms. Getting the prefix wrong is the classic beginner error, and it is always wrong by a factor of a thousand. Say the unit out loud with its prefix every time and the mistake becomes much harder to make.
What to carry out of this

When a circuit confuses you, ask the three questions in order. Where is the push coming from, and how many volts is it? What path can current take to get back to the source? What on that path limits the flow? A dead circuit usually has no push or a broken path. A hot or smoking one usually has too little resistance on the path. Beginners often chase exotic explanations. People who fix things for a living start with these three, because most faults are one of them wearing a disguise.
Two systems set your sleep

Sleep is governed by two processes working together. The first is pressure. A chemical called adenosine builds up in the brain during every hour you are awake, and the more of it there is, the sleepier you feel. Sleep clears it. The second is your body clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm that raises alertness during the day and lowers it at night regardless of how long you have been awake. You fall asleep most easily when high pressure meets a falling clock.
Light sets the clock

The clock is tuned mainly by light reaching the eyes. Bright light in the morning pulls it earlier and makes you sleepy at a sensible hour. Bright light late in the evening pushes it later. As darkness falls, the brain releases melatonin, a signal that night has begun. Indoor lighting and screens are much dimmer than daylight but still enough to delay that signal. Getting outside soon after waking is one of the most effective and least used ways to sleep better.
The night has a structure

Sleep runs in cycles of about ninety minutes. Each cycle passes through light sleep, deep sleep and a stage called REM, when most vivid dreaming occurs. The mix changes through the night. Deep sleep dominates the first half and appears to matter most for physical recovery. REM dominates the second half and is closely tied to memory and emotion. This is why cutting a night short by two hours does not cost a quarter of each stage. It removes a large share of your REM.
How much is enough

Sleep organizations recommend that most adults get at least seven hours a night, and many people function best with eight or a little more. The need varies somewhat between individuals but less than people like to think. Those who insist they are fine on five hours usually show measurable deficits when tested. A hallmark of chronic short sleep is that you stop noticing it. Your sense of your own performance levels off while your actual performance keeps falling.
What a short night costs

After 17 to 19 hours awake, reaction time and judgement in laboratory tests are impaired about as much as with a blood alcohol level of 0.05 percent, and after a full 24 hours it is worse. That is the state in which many people drive home from a long shift. Sleep also consolidates what you learned during the day, so a late night of study followed by little sleep is partly wasted. Persistent short sleep is associated with weight gain, raised blood pressure and lower mood.
The usual suspects

Caffeine works by blocking adenosine, and half of a dose is typically still in your system five or six hours later, so a late afternoon coffee is still active at bedtime. Alcohol makes you drowsy but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night and suppresses REM. A warm room interferes too, since body temperature needs to fall for sleep to begin. Most people sleep best in a room that feels slightly cool, with the feet and hands free to shed heat.
The habits that matter most

The single most useful rule is a consistent wake time, including weekends, because it anchors the clock. After that: daylight in the morning, caffeine only in the first half of the day, a dark and cool bedroom, and a bed used for sleep, not for work or scrolling. If you cannot sleep, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy. Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or tiredness that persists despite enough time in bed, is worth raising with a doctor.
Decisions you no longer make

A large share of what you do each day is not decided. You do not weigh whether to brush your teeth or which way to turn out of your street. Researchers who asked people to log their actions hour by hour have found that around four in ten were things they did almost every day in the same setting. This is efficiency, not laziness. The brain hands repeated behaviour to circuits that run it automatically, which frees attention for things that are new or difficult.
Cue, routine, reward

The standard description of a habit has three parts. A cue is the trigger: a time, a place, a feeling, a preceding action. The routine is the behaviour itself. The reward is whatever the brain gets out of it, which can be a taste, a sense of relief or simply the end of an itch. Repeat the sequence enough and the cue alone starts the routine with no deliberation. Experiments at MIT watching the brains of rats learning a maze showed the activity shrinking over time to a burst at the start and a burst at the end.
How long it takes

The popular claim that a habit takes 21 days has no good evidence behind it. A study at University College London followed people adopting a new daily behaviour, such as eating fruit with lunch or doing sit-ups after coffee. The time until it felt automatic averaged about 66 days, and individuals ranged from 18 days to 254. Simple actions settled faster than demanding ones. Missing a single day did not noticeably set anyone back, which is worth remembering the first time you slip.
Context does the work

Habits are tied to settings more than to intentions. People who move house or change jobs often find old habits loosening, because the cues have disappeared. The same fact can be used on purpose. If you want to practise guitar, leave it on a stand in the living room, not in its case in a cupboard. If you want to stop snacking, do not keep the snacks on the counter. Changing what is in front of you is usually more effective than promising yourself to try harder.
Start smaller than seems reasonable

The reliable way to install a behaviour is to make the first version almost insultingly easy. Two minutes of stretching. One page. One push-up. The point of the early weeks is not the result. It is to make the link between the cue and the action automatic. Once showing up no longer takes a decision, extending the routine is easy. People who begin with an ambitious version usually manage it until the first bad day and then stop altogether.
Replacing beats removing

A cue that has triggered a routine for years does not go quiet because you have decided it should. Breaking a habit by willpower alone leaves the cue and the craving in place with nothing to do. What tends to work better is keeping the cue and the reward and swapping in a different routine. If an afternoon slump sends you to the vending machine and what you really get from the trip is a break and a chat, a walk to a colleague's desk may serve the same need.
What to try this week

Pick one small behaviour and attach it to something you already do every day without fail. After I pour my coffee, I will write one sentence in my notebook. After I park the car, I will take three slow breaths. Keep the new action under two minutes. Do not add a second habit until the first requires no thought. It is a slow method, and its advantage over the fast ones is that people are still doing it a year later.
Interest on interest

Simple interest pays you on the amount you put in. Compound interest pays you on the amount you put in plus everything it has already earned. Put 10,000 dollars away at 7 percent a year. The first year earns 700. The second year earns 749, because the 700 is now working too. The difference seems trivial. Leave it alone for 30 years and the 10,000 becomes about 76,000. Leave it for 40 and it is about 150,000. The final ten years added as much as the first thirty.
The rule of 72

To estimate how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the annual rate of return. At 6 percent, money doubles in about 12 years. At 8 percent, about 9. At 3 percent, 24. The rule is an approximation, but a good one across the range of rates you meet in ordinary life. It also makes long horizons easy to picture. Forty years at 7 percent is roughly four doublings: one becomes two, four, eight, sixteen. The rule turns an exponent into a count on your fingers.
Why starting early beats saving more

Suppose one person invests 500 dollars a month from age 25 to 65 at a 7 percent annual return. They contribute 240,000 dollars and end with roughly 1.3 million. A second person starts at 35 and invests the same 500 a month. They contribute 180,000 and end with about 610,000. The late starter put in three quarters as much money and finished with less than half. The first ten years of deposits, given the longest time to grow, ended up being worth more than the following thirty.
The curve is flat at the start

The frustrating part of compounding is that it gives little encouragement early on. For the first decade, most of your balance is money you put in yourself. Growth is a small slice. Somewhere in the second or third decade, the growth in a single year begins to exceed what you contribute, and after that the gap widens quickly. Most people who abandon a savings plan do so in the flat part, before the curve has had the chance to show them what it does.
It works against you too

The same arithmetic runs in reverse on debt. A credit card charging 22 percent a year doubles an unpaid balance in a little over three years. A 5,000 dollar balance paid off at 100 dollars a month at that rate takes more than eleven years and costs about 13,700 dollars in total. Raise the payment to 200 a month and it is gone in under three years for about 6,750. Compounding is neutral. Whether it builds your wealth or someone else's depends on which side of the loan you stand.
Fees compound as well

A fee of 1 percent a year sounds small. Over 40 years, it is not. Ten thousand dollars growing at 7 percent becomes about 150,000. The same money growing at 6 percent, because a point is lost to fees each year, becomes about 103,000. That single percentage point consumed nearly a third of the final sum. This is the main argument for low-cost funds: you cannot control what markets return, but you can control how much of the return you hand away each year.
What to do with this

Three habits follow from the arithmetic. Start as early as you can, even with small amounts, because time does more of the work than money does. Leave the money alone, because every withdrawal removes not just the dollars but all the growth they would have produced. And pay attention to rates on both sides: chase down high-interest debt first, and keep the costs on your investments low. None of this requires skill at picking investments. It requires patience, which is rarer.
A call is a bet at fixed odds

When an opponent bets, the pot is offering you a wager. You put in a known amount for the chance to win what is already out there. Pot odds are just that ratio: the money you can win compared with the money you must pay. Suppose the pot holds 100 dollars and your opponent bets 50. There is now 150 to win and it costs you 50 to try. You are getting 150 to 50, or 3 to 1. Nothing about your cards has entered the picture yet. This is purely the price.
Turn the price into a percentage

Odds of 3 to 1 mean that out of four tries, you can lose three and win one and break even. So you need to win one time in four, or 25 percent. The quick formula is the size of your call divided by the total pot after you call. Here that is 50 divided by 200, which is 25 percent. If your hand will win more often than that, calling makes money over time. If it will win less often, calling loses money, no matter how the hand feels.
Memorize four bet sizes

You do not need to calculate at the table if you learn the common cases. Facing a bet of one third of the pot, you need 20 percent. Facing half the pot, 25 percent. Facing two thirds, about 29 percent. Facing a bet the full size of the pot, 33 percent. A bet of twice the pot demands 40 percent. Notice how gently the requirement rises. Even a huge overbet never asks you to be a favourite. It only asks you to win often enough to pay for the times you lose.
A worked example with a draw

You hold two hearts and by the turn the board shows two more. One card is left to come, and nine hearts remain among the 46 cards you cannot see. You will complete the flush about 19.6 percent of the time on that last card. Your opponent bets 50 into 100, so you need 25 percent. A flush draw alone is not enough at that price. Had the bet been 25 into 100, you would need only one sixth, about 16.7 percent, and the call would be correct.
Why small bets are hard to fold to

Pot odds explain a feeling every player knows: small bets are annoying. A bet of a quarter of the pot offers 5 to 1, so you need to win barely 17 percent of the time. Many weak hands clear that bar. This is why good players do not fold everything to a tiny bet, and why betting small with a strong hand that wants a call is often correct. The size of the bet, as much as the cards, decides how wide the caller can profitably be.
What pot odds leave out

The basic sum assumes the hand ends after your call. Often it does not. If more cards and more bets are coming, you may win extra money when you hit, which improves the deal, or face another bet when you miss, which worsens it. Those adjustments have their own names, implied odds and reverse implied odds. Pot odds are the starting point: the honest price right now. Skilled players start there and then adjust for what is likely to happen on later streets.
Make it a habit

Before every call, say the price to yourself: what is in the pot, what does it cost, what percentage is that. Then ask how often your hand wins. Most losing players skip the first half and go straight to hoping. The habit takes a few sessions to become automatic, and it removes the most expensive leak in casual poker, which is calling too often with hands that cannot win enough of the time to justify the price.
Books before printing

Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe was copied by hand. A scribe might take months over a single Bible. Books were therefore rare, expensive and concentrated in monasteries, universities and the houses of the rich. A scholar's personal library might hold a few dozen volumes. Copying also introduced errors, so that no two copies of a work were quite the same, and each generation of copies drifted a little further from the original. A large monastery library was a treasure counted in hundreds of books.
What Gutenberg actually invented

Printing itself was not new. Chinese printers had used carved wooden blocks for centuries, and movable type made from clay and later metal existed in China and Korea well before 1450. Johannes Gutenberg's achievement was a complete, practical system. He devised a hand mould that could cast large numbers of identical metal letters quickly, an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that cast cleanly, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from those used for wine and olives.
The first great book

Gutenberg's Bible was finished in Mainz around 1455. About 180 copies were made, some on vellum and most on paper, each with 42 lines to the page. It was a commercial venture and it ruined him. His financial backer, Johann Fust, sued for repayment as the project neared completion and took over the workshop. Gutenberg died in 1468 without having profited much from the invention that carries his name. Around fifty of the Bibles survive, in whole or in part.
The speed of the spread

The technology escaped Mainz almost at once. By 1500, less than fifty years later, presses were operating in well over two hundred European towns, and historians estimate that something like twenty million volumes had been printed. The price of a book fell steeply. A press could turn out in a day what a scribe produced in months. For the first time, a scholar in Kraków and one in Lisbon could be reasonably sure they were reading the same text, page for page.
Religion and revolt

The first large demonstration of the press's power was religious. When Martin Luther circulated his criticisms of the Church in 1517, printers reproduced them within weeks, and his later pamphlets sold in the hundreds of thousands. Earlier reformers had been contained because their ideas travelled no faster than a manuscript. Luther's could not be contained. The Reformation, and the wars that followed it, are hard to imagine without cheap print. The same presses served his opponents just as readily.
Science and standard knowledge

Printing changed what knowledge was. Tables of numbers, maps and anatomical drawings could now be reproduced exactly, which they never could by hand. Errors could be corrected in a second edition and stay corrected. Scholars could build on one another's work across a continent, because they were all looking at the same pages. Copernicus on the heavens and Vesalius on the human body both published in 1543. The scientific revolution was, among other things, a consequence of dependable copies.
The pattern to notice

The press is the classic case of a technology that makes copying cheap. The results were not all benign. It spread astrology, witch-hunting manuals and forged news alongside scripture and science, and authorities struggled for a century to control it with licences and lists of banned books. But the long-run effect was that ideas became far harder to suppress and literacy became worth having. When a later technology makes copying cheaper again, this is the precedent people reach for.
The rule itself

Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance. Write it V equals I times R, where I is the old symbol for current. Rearranged, current is voltage divided by resistance, and resistance is voltage divided by current. Cover the one you want and the other two show you what to do. Twelve volts across 6 ohms gives 2 amps. Five volts pushing 0.5 amps means 10 ohms. Georg Ohm published the relationship in 1827 and was mocked for it. Nearly two centuries later it is the first thing anyone checks.
Think in milliamps and kilohms

Small circuits rarely deal in whole amps. They deal in milliamps, thousandths of an amp, and kilohms, thousands of ohms. Those two units cancel neatly. Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps directly. Five volts across 10 kilohms is 0.5 milliamps. Three point three volts across 1 kilohm is 3.3 milliamps. Keep the units paired like that and you can do most bench arithmetic in your head. Mix amps with kilohms and you will be off by a factor of a thousand, the most common mistake a beginner makes.
The classic example: an LED

A red LED wants about 20 milliamps and drops about 2 volts when lit. You have a 5 volt supply. The resistor in series must soak up the other 3 volts while passing 20 milliamps. Three volts divided by 20 milliamps is 0.15 kilohms, or 150 ohms. The nearest common value above that is 220 ohms, which gives a slightly dimmer and longer lived LED. That thirty second calculation is the one you will do most often in hobby electronics, and it is nothing but Ohm's law applied to the leftover voltage.
Use it to find faults

Ohm's law also works backwards as a detective. If a resistor marked 100 ohms measures 4 volts across it, 40 milliamps must be flowing through it, whether or not the design intended that. Measuring voltage across a known resistance is how technicians find current without cutting a wire. If the number is far from what the design expects, something upstream is wrong. A voltage that should be there and is not, or a current that is much too high, points you toward the fault faster than staring at the board.
Where the law runs out

Ohm's law describes parts whose resistance stays put, such as resistors and wires. Many parts do not behave that way. A diode passes almost nothing until about 0.6 volts and then conducts freely. A light bulb filament has ten times more resistance hot than cold. A transistor changes its resistance on command, which is the whole point of it. For those parts you still use the law, but on one operating point at a time, with numbers taken from the datasheet, not from one fixed resistance.
The same law explains wire sizes

Wire has resistance too, small but real. A thin wire carrying a large current loses voltage along its length, and the loss is current times the wire's resistance. Ten amps through a cable with a tenth of an ohm of resistance drops a full volt before the power reaches the load, and the cable warms up doing it. That is why jumper cables are as thick as a thumb, why long runs of low voltage garden lighting dim at the far end, and why electricians choose wire gauge by the current it must carry.
A habit worth building

Before you connect power to anything, estimate the current. Take the supply voltage, divide by the smallest resistance on the path, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Five volts into 220 ohms is about 23 milliamps, fine. Five volts into a wire with nothing else on the path is whatever the supply can deliver, which means a short circuit. The estimate takes five seconds and saves parts, batteries and fingertips. People who do this every time rarely see smoke. People who skip it meet smoke early and often.
Why bother

Muscle is not just for appearance. It moves you, protects joints, stores and burns fuel, and keeps you independent in old age. From roughly the fourth decade of life, adults who do nothing lose muscle steadily, a few percent each decade and faster after sixty. Strength falls faster still. Resistance training slows and partly reverses that decline at any age, including in people in their eighties and nineties. Health guidelines recommend working all the major muscle groups at least twice a week.
The one principle

Everything in strength training follows from a single idea called progressive overload. The body adapts to demands slightly greater than those it is used to. Ask a muscle to do a little more than last time, give it time to recover, and it comes back slightly stronger. Ask it to do the same thing forever and it stays the same. More can mean more weight, more repetitions, more sets or better control. If the numbers in your training log never change, neither will you.
A handful of movements

You do not need dozens of exercises. Most of the body can be trained with a few basic patterns: a squat, a hip hinge such as a deadlift, a push such as a press-up or bench press, a pull such as a row or pull-up, and carrying something heavy. These movements use several joints and many muscles together, which makes them efficient. Machines, free weights, resistance bands and body weight all work. The best equipment is whichever kind you have access to and will actually use. A pair of adjustable dumbbells and a doorway pull-up bar are enough to train for years at home.
How hard, how much

A set should finish with the last few repetitions being genuinely difficult, leaving perhaps one to three more in reserve. Research shows muscle can be built across a wide range of repetitions, from about five to thirty, as long as the effort is high. Lower repetitions with heavier weights favour maximal strength. For most people, two to four sets of each movement, two or three times a week, is enough to make steady progress for years.
Recovery is when you grow

Training provides the signal. The adaptation happens afterwards. A muscle group generally needs about two days before it is trained hard again, which is why programmes alternate body parts or schedule rest days. Sleep and sufficient protein matter as much as anything you do in the gym. Soreness a day or two after a new exercise is normal and fades as the body adapts. It is not a measure of how effective the session was.
Technique and safety

Learn each movement with a light load and add weight only when you can control it through the full range. Progress slowly. Adding a small amount each week accumulates into a large change over a year. Sharp or joint pain, as opposed to the dull effort of working muscle, is a signal to stop and reassess. A session or two with a qualified coach at the start is money well spent. Anyone with a heart condition or other medical concern should check with a clinician first.
What to expect

Beginners improve quickly. Much of the early gain is the nervous system learning to use muscle you already have, which is why strength rises before any visible change. After several months, progress slows and patience becomes the main requirement. The people with the best results after five years are seldom those who followed the cleverest programme. They are the ones who kept turning up twice a week, wrote down what they lifted and tried to do slightly more.
The gap between meaning to and doing

Most people who fail to exercise, save or study intended to do it. Researchers call this the intention to behaviour gap. Wanting something, even strongly, turns out to predict what people actually do far less well than you might expect. The trouble is rarely motivation. It is that when the moment arrives, you are tired or distracted, the opportunity passes unnoticed, or something more appealing is in front of you. Goals are set in calm conditions and carried out in messy ones.
The format

The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer proposed a remedy in the 1990s and called it an implementation intention. Instead of a goal such as I will exercise more, you write a plan in the form: if situation X arises, then I will do Y. If it is Monday, Wednesday or Friday at 7 in the morning, then I will put on my running shoes and go out the door. The plan names a specific cue and a specific first action. Nothing more is needed.
The evidence

The results have been repeated many times. In one British study, people were asked to exercise at least once in the following week. A group given only information did so about 38 percent of the time. A group given extra motivational material managed about 35 percent. A third group also wrote down when and where they would exercise, and 91 percent followed through. A later review covering 94 separate studies found a consistent and sizeable benefit across health, study and work goals.
Why it works

Deciding in advance does two things. It makes the cue stand out, so that when 7 o'clock comes or you pass the gym, you notice it. And it links the cue to the action so that the response begins without a fresh debate. The decision has already been made by a calmer version of you. In the moment there is nothing to negotiate. The effect resembles a habit installed by a single act of planning instead of by months of repetition.
Plans for obstacles

The format is even more useful for the moments that usually derail you. If I feel like skipping the session, then I will do just the first five minutes. If someone offers me a drink, then I will ask for sparkling water. If I open my phone during work, then I will close it and write down what I was avoiding. Identifying your most likely point of failure and writing a response to it in advance is sometimes called coping planning, and studies that combine it with an ordinary plan generally find the pair works better than either alone.
Where it falls short

An if-then plan is not a spell. It works best when you genuinely hold the goal and when the cue is concrete: a time, a place or a preceding action. Vague cues such as when I have a free moment do little. Too many plans at once dilute each other. And a plan cannot overcome a goal you do not actually want, which is worth noticing. If you repeatedly ignore a well-made plan, the honest question may be whether the goal is really yours.
Write one now

Choose one thing you have been meaning to do. Write a single sentence that states the day, the time, the place and the first physical action. Put it somewhere you will see it. Then write one more sentence for the obstacle most likely to stop you. That is the whole technique. It takes about a minute, costs nothing, and has better evidence behind it than most of what is sold as self-improvement.
What an index fund is

A stock index is a list of companies chosen by a rule, such as the 500 large American companies in the S&P 500. An index fund simply buys every company on the list in the same proportions and holds them. It makes no attempt to pick winners or avoid losers. The first index fund open to ordinary investors was launched by John Bogle at Vanguard in 1976. Competitors mocked it as a guarantee of mediocrity. It became one of the most influential financial products ever created.
The arithmetic of average

The case rests on a piece of logic. All investors together own the whole market, so before costs, the average investor must earn the market's return. After costs, the average investor earns the market's return minus what they paid in fees and trading. An index fund charges very little, often a few hundredths of a percent a year. A typical actively managed fund charges far more. So the low-cost index fund must beat the average actively managed dollar, simply by subtraction.
What the scorecards show

The data matches the logic. S&P publishes a regular scorecard comparing actively managed funds with their benchmark indexes. Over periods of fifteen years or longer, the large majority of American stock funds have trailed the index, typically more than eight in ten. Some managers do win. The trouble is that it is very hard to tell in advance which ones, and funds that led in one period have shown little tendency to lead in the next.
Most stocks are duds

There is a deeper reason picking is hard. A well-known study by the finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder examined American stocks from 1926 to 2016. More than half of all stocks did worse over their lifetimes than short-term government bills. Just over 4 percent of companies accounted for all of the market's net gain. The market's return comes from a small number of huge winners. Owning everything guarantees you hold them. Picking a handful makes it likely you miss them.
What it does not protect you from

An index fund is not safe in the sense of never falling. It falls exactly as far as the market does. American stocks lost roughly half their value in the crisis of 2007 to 2009 and index investors lost with them. What the fund removes is the extra risk of having chosen badly: the single company that collapses, the manager who loses their touch. The risk that remains is the risk of the market itself, and the only tools for that are time and a mix that includes safer assets.
The behaviour gap

The hardest part of index investing is doing nothing. Studies of fund investors repeatedly find that people earn less than the funds they own, because they buy after prices have risen and sell after they have fallen. An index fund cannot stop you from doing that. The investors who actually collect the market return are those who keep buying on a schedule and do not look too often. The strategy is simple to understand and difficult to follow, which is different from being complicated.
How people use them

A common approach is a small number of broad funds: one covering domestic stocks, one covering international stocks and one covering bonds, in proportions that suit your age and nerves. Target date funds package this mix and adjust it as retirement approaches. The details vary by country and by account type, and they are worth getting right with a qualified adviser if the sums are large. The underlying idea does not change: own broadly, pay little, and let time do the work.
What an out is

An out is any unseen card that turns your hand into the likely winner. If you hold four cards to a flush, there are thirteen cards of that suit in the deck, you can see four, so nine remain. Those nine are your outs. An open-ended straight draw, such as 8 and 9 on a board of 7, 10 and a king, can be completed by any six or any jack: eight outs. A gutshot, needing one specific rank in the middle, has four. Counting outs is the first step in knowing what a draw is worth.
The shortcut

With one card to come, multiply your outs by two to get the approximate percentage chance of hitting. With two cards to come, on the flop, multiply by four. A flush draw with nine outs has roughly 18 percent on the next card and roughly 36 percent by the river. The true figures are 19.6 percent with one card left and 35 percent with two. The shortcut works because each unseen card is about 2 percent of the deck you cannot see.
The numbers worth knowing cold

Four outs, a gutshot: about 9 percent on one card and 16.5 percent with two. Six outs, two overcards hoping to pair: about 13 and 24 percent. Eight outs, the open-ended straight draw: about 17 and 31.5 percent. Nine outs, the flush draw: about 19.6 and 35 percent. Fifteen outs, a straight and flush draw combined: about 33 percent on one card and 54 percent with two. That last hand is a favourite over a made pair, which surprises many players the first time they see it.
Fix the shortcut for big draws

The rule of four overstates large draws. Fifteen outs times four is 60, but the real figure is 54 percent. The correction is simple: when you have more than eight outs, take the number of outs above eight and subtract it from your answer. Fifteen is seven more than eight, and 60 minus 7 is 53, within a point of the truth. For draws of eight outs or fewer the plain rule is accurate enough that no fix is needed.
Not every out is clean

Some cards that complete your hand also complete a better one for someone else. If you hold a straight draw on a board with two spades, the two cards that make your straight in spades may hand an opponent a flush. If you hope to pair your ace against someone holding ace king, that pair leaves you second best. Experienced players discount tainted outs, counting a doubtful card as half an out or none. Overcounting outs is the most common way a draw gets overvalued.
Use four only when you see both cards

The rule of four assumes you will see the turn and the river for the price you pay now. That is only true if you or your opponent is all in on the flop. If there is more betting to come, your opponent can charge you again on the turn, and you should compare the bet in front of you with your chance on the next card alone, the rule of two. Using four on the flop when another bet is coming is how players talk themselves into bad calls.
Put it together with the price

The method is two numbers side by side. Count your clean outs and convert them to a percentage. Work out the percentage the pot is asking for. If the first is bigger, continue. If it is smaller, fold, unless you expect to win a lot more when you hit. With practice the whole comparison takes two or three seconds. It replaces the vague sense that a draw is promising with a figure, and the figure is right far more often than the feeling.
Bad air

Until the late nineteenth century, the leading explanation for epidemic disease was miasma: poisonous vapour rising from rotting matter, swamps and filth. The word malaria means bad air. The theory was not foolish. Disease really did cluster where things smelled bad, and cleaning up cities really did help. But it was wrong about the mechanism, and so it gave no reason for a doctor to wash their hands or sterilize their instruments, since the air was the same for everyone.
Semmelweis and the hands

In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian doctor in Vienna, noticed that women giving birth in the ward staffed by medical students died of fever far more often than those in the ward staffed by midwives. The students came to deliveries straight from dissecting corpses. He ordered them to wash their hands in a chlorine solution, and deaths in his ward fell from well over ten percent to around two. His colleagues took offence at the idea that they were the cause. He lost his post and died in an asylum in 1865.
Snow and the pump

In 1854, cholera struck the Soho district of London. The physician John Snow plotted the deaths on a street map and found them clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer, were spared. Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump handle. He could not say what in the water was responsible, but he had shown the disease travelled by water and not by air. His map is regarded as a founding document of epidemiology.
Pasteur's flasks

The decisive experiments came from the French chemist Louis Pasteur in the 1860s. He boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but trapped dust. The broth stayed clear indefinitely. When he broke a neck or tilted the flask so the liquid touched the trapped dust, it soon swarmed with microbes. Life was not arising spontaneously from the broth. It was arriving from outside. Pasteur went on to show that microbes spoil wine and milk, and that gentle heating prevents it.
Lister in the operating theatre

The Scottish surgeon Joseph Lister read Pasteur and drew the obvious conclusion. If microbes cause rot, perhaps they cause the infections that killed so many patients after surgery. In the 1860s he began treating wounds, instruments and dressings with carbolic acid. Deaths after amputation on his wards dropped sharply. Surgeons of the time operated in coats stiff with old blood, a mark of experience. Within a generation, clean hands, sterile instruments and eventually gowns and gloves had become the rule.
Koch names the culprits

The German doctor Robert Koch supplied the final step: proof that a specific microbe causes a specific disease. He identified the bacterium behind anthrax in 1876 and the one behind tuberculosis in 1882, then the cause of cholera. He set out a method that became known as Koch's postulates: find the organism in every case, grow it in pure culture, show that it causes the disease in a healthy animal, and recover it again. Medicine now had a way to hunt.
What followed

Few ideas have saved more lives. Clean water and sewers, pasteurized milk, antiseptic surgery, vaccines and eventually antibiotics all rest on germ theory. Life expectancy in industrial countries roughly doubled in the century and a half that followed, and control of infectious disease accounts for a large part of that. It is worth remembering how recently it was resisted. The doctors who dismissed Semmelweis were not stupid. They were being asked to believe in a killer they could not see.
Power is volts times amps

Power, measured in watts, is how fast energy is being used. In a circuit it is voltage multiplied by current. A phone charger delivering 5 volts at 2 amps supplies 10 watts. A 12 volt car headlamp drawing 5 amps uses 60 watts. Substituting Ohm's law gives two more forms: current squared times resistance, and voltage squared divided by resistance. All three give the same answer. Pick whichever uses the two numbers you already know, and you can find the power in any part of a circuit.
Every part has a limit

A resistor does not just have a resistance. It has a power rating, the heat it can shed without cooking. The common small through-hole resistor is rated a quarter of a watt. Put 5 volts across a 100 ohm one and it dissipates 25 divided by 100, a quarter of a watt, right at its limit and too hot to touch. Put 12 volts across it and it must shed 1.44 watts. It will brown, smell and fail. The value was right. The size was wrong.
Why the square matters

Because power rises with the square of current, small increases hurt more than you expect. Double the current through a wire and it makes four times the heat. Triple it and you get nine times. This is why an extension cord that runs a lamp happily gets dangerously warm feeding a space heater, and why power companies send electricity long distances at very high voltage. For the same power, higher voltage means lower current, and lower current means far less energy wasted heating the wires along the way.
Leave yourself a margin

Good practice is to run parts at no more than about half their rating. If a resistor will dissipate 0.2 watts, use a half watt part. The same thinking applies to capacitors and voltage, to transistors and current, and to power supplies. A part run at its limit works on the bench and fails in a closed box on a hot day, because ratings assume air at room temperature moving freely. Derating, as engineers call it, is the cheapest reliability you can buy.
Getting the heat out

When a part must handle real power, the design job becomes moving heat away. That is what the finned metal heatsinks on amplifiers and voltage regulators do. They give the heat more surface to leave from. A fan helps further by replacing the warm air. Thermal paste fills the microscopic gaps between a chip and its heatsink, because air is a poor conductor of heat. A regulator that shuts down after ten minutes is usually not broken. It is hot, and it is protecting itself.
Batteries are a power budget

Power thinking also tells you how long a battery lasts. A battery's capacity is given in amp hours or milliamp hours, the current it can supply multiplied by the time. A 2,000 milliamp hour cell feeding a circuit that draws 100 milliamps lasts roughly 20 hours. Multiply capacity by voltage and you get watt hours, the honest measure of stored energy and the number airlines use to limit what you can carry on. If a gadget dies early, measure what it draws while asleep. A forgotten 5 milliamps runs all day, every day.
The check to run

For any part that feels warm, work out the power. Measure the voltage across it and the current through it, multiply, and compare with the rating on the datasheet. If you are above half, change something: a larger part, a higher resistance, a lower voltage or a heatsink. Smell is also a tool. Overheated resistors and circuit boards have a sharp, sweet, burnt odour that people who repair electronics learn to recognize from across a room. If you smell it, cut the power first and investigate second.
What fitness means here

Cardiorespiratory fitness is your body's ability to take in oxygen and deliver it to working muscles. It is commonly expressed as VO2 max, the greatest amount of oxygen you can use in a minute of all-out effort. Large studies following people for many years have found it to be one of the strongest predictors of how long they live, comparable to or stronger than better-known risk factors. The largest improvement in outlook comes from moving out of the least fit group, not from becoming an athlete.
The guideline

The World Health Organization and national health bodies recommend that adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity each week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mixture. Moderate means brisk walking, easy cycling or anything that raises your breathing while still allowing conversation. Vigorous means running, fast cycling or anything that reduces you to a few words at a time. One minute of vigorous effort counts for about two of moderate.
The talk test

You do not need a monitor to judge intensity. If you can speak in full sentences but could not sing, you are working at a moderate level. If you can only manage short phrases, it is vigorous. If you can sing, it is light. For those who do track heart rate, a common estimate of maximum is 220 minus your age, though for any individual that figure can be off by ten beats or more. Treat it as a rough guide, not a limit.
Easy most of the time

Endurance athletes do the bulk of their training at a comfortable, conversational effort, often called zone 2. Work at this level builds the heart's capacity to pump, increases the number of small blood vessels in muscle and multiplies the mitochondria that turn fuel into energy. It can be repeated day after day with little risk of injury or burnout. Beginners often go too hard in every session, which feels productive and makes it difficult to do enough total volume.
Hard some of the time

A smaller amount of high-intensity work raises the ceiling. Intervals, such as four minutes hard followed by a few minutes easy, repeated several times, are a well-studied way to increase VO2 max. One or two such sessions a week is plenty for most people. A split often quoted by coaches is about 80 percent easy and 20 percent hard. The easy work builds the base and the hard work sharpens it. Either alone does less than the combination.
Sitting and moving

Formal exercise is only part of the picture. Long unbroken hours of sitting are associated with poorer health even among people who exercise, and breaking them up with a few minutes of walking helps. Everyday movement counts: stairs, errands on foot, gardening. Studies of step counts suggest the benefits rise steeply from very low numbers and begin to level off well before the famous figure of ten thousand, which began as a marketing slogan for a Japanese pedometer in the 1960s.
Getting started

If you are doing nothing now, begin with a ten-minute brisk walk each day and add five minutes a week. Pick something you do not hate, because the best exercise is the one you repeat. Increase your weekly total gradually, by about a tenth at a time, to let tendons and joints keep pace with your lungs. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness during exertion are reasons to stop and seek medical advice, as is starting from a long-standing medical condition.
Multitasking is switching

When you believe you are doing two mentally demanding things at once, you are in fact alternating between them. Each switch has a cost. The brain must set aside one set of rules and load another. Laboratory tasks show people becoming both slower and more error-prone when they alternate, compared with finishing one task and then the other. The loss on each switch is a fraction of a second, but the fractions accumulate, and the errors rise with the complexity of the work.
The residue

The business researcher Sophie Leroy gave the lingering cost a name: attention residue. When you leave a task unfinished and turn to another, part of your mind stays with the first. In her experiments, people who had been interrupted performed worse on the next task than those allowed to finish. The residue is thickest when the abandoned task was absorbing and incomplete. This is why a quick glance at email in the middle of hard thinking is never as quick as it looks.
The price of an interruption

Field studies of office workers, including well-known work by Gloria Mark, found that people switched what they were doing every few minutes, and that after a real interruption it took on average over twenty minutes to get back to the original task. Often they passed through two other tasks on the way. About half of the interruptions were self-inflicted. Nobody had knocked or called. The worker had simply reached for something else.
Why you reach for the phone

Self-interruption is not a failure of character. Difficult thinking is mildly unpleasant, and the brain looks for relief. A phone offers a reliable small reward within a second or two. Notifications make it worse by supplying a cue you did not ask for. One much-discussed study found that having your own phone visible on the desk, face down and silent, slightly reduced performance on demanding tasks, though attempts to repeat the result have been mixed. Either way, a phone within reach is a cue you have to keep refusing.
Design beats discipline

Because the pull is constant, resisting it by willpower is exhausting and unreliable. Removing the cue works better. Put the phone in another room. Close the email program entirely instead of minimizing it. Turn off every notification that is not from a person who needs you now. Work in full-screen mode. These changes feel trivial and have large effects, because they remove dozens of small decisions an hour. You stop resisting temptation because the temptation is not there.
Work in blocks

The other half is scheduling. Set aside a block of time, an hour or ninety minutes, for one demanding task and nothing else. Decide beforehand exactly what you will work on. Batch email and messages into a few set times instead of answering as they arrive. Many people find that two or three protected blocks produce more than an entire day of fragmented effort. Few people can sustain more than about four hours of truly concentrated work in a day, so guard those hours.
Rest is part of it

Sustained focus needs recovery. Short breaks that actually rest the mind, such as a walk, looking out of a window or a conversation, restore concentration better than breaks spent scrolling, which keep demanding attention. Sleep matters more than any technique. A tired brain switches more, resists less and makes more mistakes. If you want to concentrate better tomorrow, the most effective step may be the unglamorous one of going to bed on time tonight.
Two kinds of risk

A share of a single company can fall for reasons specific to that company. A product fails, an accounting scandal breaks, a rival wins. It can also fall because the whole market falls, in a recession or a panic. The first kind is called specific risk and the second market risk. The distinction matters because one of them can be removed nearly for free. Hold enough different companies and the individual disasters and windfalls largely cancel out. Market risk remains however many you hold.
The only free lunch

The economist Harry Markowitz showed in the 1950s that the risk of a portfolio depends not just on how risky each holding is but on how the holdings move in relation to one another. Two assets that do not rise and fall together produce a combination that is steadier than either alone. He later shared a Nobel Prize for the work, and the idea is often summed up in a line attributed to him: diversification is the only free lunch in investing.
An umbrella and sunscreen

Picture a beach stall that sells only sunscreen. It does well in sunny weeks and badly in wet ones. A stall selling only umbrellas has the opposite problem. A stall that sells both earns a steadier income, though neither product has become any less dependent on the weather. That is diversification in miniature. The benefit comes from the two not moving together. Owning ten companies in the same industry is like stocking ten brands of sunscreen and calling it variety.
What counts as different

Real diversification means holding things that respond differently to the same events. Companies in different industries. Companies in different countries. Different kinds of asset: shares, bonds, property, cash. High-quality government bonds have often risen when shares fell sharply, which is why the two are so commonly paired, though this has not held in every period. In 2022, for example, both fell together as interest rates rose quickly. Diversification improves the odds. It does not issue guarantees.
Volatility is not the whole of risk

Finance usually measures risk as volatility, how much a price bounces around. It is a convenient yardstick but an incomplete one. For a person, the real risks are needing money when prices are down, and being frightened into selling at the bottom. A portfolio that swings wildly is only dangerous if you will be forced, by circumstance or by nerves, to sell during a swing. This is why money needed within a few years does not belong in shares, however good the long-run averages look.
Concentration cuts both ways

Almost every great fortune was built through concentration: one company, one property, one idea. That is what survivorship looks like. For each founder who became rich holding a single stock, many others held a single stock that went to zero, and you do not hear from them. Employees who keep their savings in their employer's shares are doubly exposed, since a bad year can take the job and the savings at once. Concentration is how wealth is made. Diversification is how it is kept.
Putting it to use

The practical version is undramatic. Hold broad funds instead of a few names. Mix assets according to when you will need the money. Check once or twice a year whether one part has grown to dominate, and if so, trim it back toward your intended mix, a habit called rebalancing. Accept that a diversified portfolio will always contain something that is doing badly. That is not a flaw in the design. It is the evidence that the design is working.
A share, not a verdict

Equity is the percentage of the time your hand will win if all the remaining cards are dealt with no more betting. If you would win 60 times in 100, you have 60 percent equity, and 60 percent of the pot is yours in the long-run sense. On any single deal you win everything or nothing. Over thousands of deals the results converge on the share. Thinking this way separates the quality of a decision from the luck of one outcome.
The match-ups to memorize

A few preflop confrontations come up constantly. A higher pair against a lower pair, such as aces against kings, is roughly an 80 to 20 favourite. A pair against two higher cards, queens against ace king, is close to even, about 55 to 45 for the pair. That is the classic coin flip. A hand that shares a card with a better kicker, ace king against ace queen, is about a 70 to 30 favourite. Two higher cards against two lower ones, ace king against 7 6, is only around 60 to 40.
Nothing is ever dead before the flop

The striking thing about those numbers is how much the weaker hand keeps. The worst common match-up, an underpair against an overpair, still wins about one time in five. Seven two offsuit, the worst starting hand, wins roughly one time in nine against a pair of aces. This is why all-in pots before the flop swing so wildly and why a single lost coin flip tells you nothing about how you played. The cards to come carry a great deal of the result.
Equity moves with every card

Your share is recalculated each time a card lands. Ace king against a pair of queens starts at about 45 percent. If the flop comes without an ace or a king, it falls to roughly 24 percent, because you now have six outs and two cards to come. If an ace lands, the positions reverse and the queens are left with two outs, around 8 percent. Strong players track this as the board develops. The hand you started with matters less on each street than the share you hold now.
Betting is about denying or charging

Once you think in shares, the reason to bet with a good hand becomes clear. An opponent with a flush draw owns about a third of the pot on the flop. If you check and let them see cards for free, they collect that share at no cost. If you bet, they must either pay more than their share is worth or fold and surrender it. Giving free cards to hands with real equity is one of the quietest ways to lose money.
Equity against a range

You never know your opponent's exact cards, so real equity is measured against the whole set of hands they could hold. Against someone who only raises with aces, kings, queens and ace king, a pair of jacks has only about 36 percent. Against someone raising a wide assortment of hands, the same jacks may have 65 percent. The cards have not changed. The opponent has. That is why the same hand can be a fold against one player and a confident raise against another.
Practise away from the table

Free equity calculators let you enter two hands, or a hand against a range, and see the shares. Spending twenty minutes entering the situations you were unsure about is the fastest way to build intuition. After a few weeks you stop guessing. You simply know that a pair plus a flush draw is around 50 percent against top pair, that two overcards and a gutshot have about 40 percent, and that a bare gutshot is seldom worth chasing.
A jigsaw puzzle on the map

Anyone who looks at a world map notices that the east coast of South America seems to fit against the west coast of Africa. In 1912, a German meteorologist named Alfred Wegener proposed that this was no coincidence. The continents, he argued, had once been joined in a single landmass, which he called Pangaea, and had since drifted apart. He gathered evidence for it over the following years and published his case in a book in 1915.
Wegener's evidence

The fit of the coastlines was only the start. Fossils of the same land animals and plants turned up on continents now separated by thousands of kilometres of ocean, including a small freshwater reptile found in both Brazil and southern Africa. Mountain belts and rock formations matched across the Atlantic like torn newspaper. Deposits left by glaciers lay in places now tropical. Wegener argued that it was simpler to move the continents than to explain all of this any other way.
Why he was dismissed

Geologists of the day mostly rejected the idea, some with open scorn. Wegener was an outsider to their field, and more importantly, he could not explain what force could push a continent through solid ocean floor. The mechanisms he suggested were shown to be far too weak. He died in 1930 on an expedition to the Greenland ice cap, his theory still regarded as a curiosity. He had the right answer and the wrong explanation for it.
The sea floor speaks

The evidence that revived the idea came from the oceans. After the Second World War, ships with sonar mapped the sea bed in detail for the first time. Marie Tharp, working with Bruce Heezen in New York, drew maps that revealed a vast mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, with a deep valley along its crest. In the early 1960s, Harry Hess proposed that new sea floor was being created at such ridges and spreading outward on both sides.
Magnetic stripes

The proof arrived in 1963. The Earth's magnetic field has reversed direction many times, and volcanic rock records the direction of the field at the moment it cools. Surveys found that the sea floor on either side of a ridge is striped with bands of alternating magnetism, and that the pattern on one side is a mirror image of the other. Only one explanation fits: rock forms at the ridge, records the field, and moves away as newer rock takes its place. By the late 1960s, the argument was over.
How the plates behave

The modern picture is that the Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into a dozen or so large plates that ride on hotter, slowly flowing rock beneath. They move a few centimetres a year. Where they pull apart, new crust forms. Where they collide, one may dive beneath the other, producing deep trenches, volcanoes and the largest earthquakes, or the crust may crumple upward, as it did when India ran into Asia and raised the Himalayas. Where they slide past each other, as along California's San Andreas Fault, the ground lurches.
One theory, many answers

Plate tectonics explains at a stroke why earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow belts, why the Pacific is ringed with both, why mountains stand where they do and why similar fossils appear on separate continents. It does for geology what evolution does for biology. The story also carries a lesson about science. A correct idea was rejected for decades for want of a mechanism, and it was new instruments and new data, not persuasion, that changed minds.
One path or several

Parts are in series when they sit end to end on a single path, so the same current has to pass through each in turn. Parts are in parallel when they connect across the same two points, so each gets the same voltage and the current splits between them. Old strings of holiday lights were wired in series, which is why one dead bulb darkened the lot. The sockets in your house are wired in parallel, which is why switching off a lamp does not switch off the refrigerator.
Series: resistance adds, voltage divides

In series, resistances add. A 100 ohm and a 220 ohm resistor in series behave as 320 ohms. The same current flows through both, and the supply voltage is shared between them in proportion to their values, with the bigger resistor taking the bigger share. On a 3.2 volt supply, that pair would pass 10 milliamps, with 1 volt across the first and 2.2 across the second. The shares always add up to the supply. That bookkeeping rule is called Kirchhoff's voltage law.
Parallel: more paths, less resistance

In parallel, adding a resistor always lowers the total resistance, because you have opened another path. Two equal resistors in parallel make half of one. Two 1 kilohm resistors give 500 ohms. For unequal values, multiply the two and divide by their sum. A 1 kilohm and a 3 kilohm pair gives 750 ohms. The total is always smaller than the smallest branch. Each branch draws its own current as if the others were not there, and the supply must provide the sum.
Batteries follow the same logic

Cells in series add their voltages. Four 1.5 volt AA cells end to end make 6 volts, with the same capacity as one cell. Cells in parallel keep the voltage of one but add their capacities, so the pack lasts longer or delivers more current. Laptop and electric car packs combine both, with groups of parallel cells stacked in series. Mixing old and new cells is a bad idea in either arrangement, because the weaker cell gets driven by the stronger ones, heats up and can leak.
Why overloaded outlets trip

Every appliance plugged into a household circuit is in parallel with the others. Each one adds its current to the total flowing through the wire in the wall. A kettle and a toaster together can draw more than the wire is rated to carry. The circuit breaker exists to notice that total and open the loop before the wire overheats. So a tripped breaker is not a fault in any one appliance. It is the sum of the parallel branches exceeding what the shared wire can safely handle.
Capacitors do the opposite

Resistors add in series and shrink in parallel. Capacitors do the reverse. Two capacitors in parallel simply add, because you have made a bigger tank. Two in series give less than either one, using the same multiply and divide by the sum rule that parallel resistors use. That is why you often see several small capacitors side by side on a board: together they act as one larger part, and they respond faster than a single big one would. Knowing which rule belongs to which part saves a lot of confusion later.
Reading a real circuit

Real circuits mix both arrangements, and the skill is spotting which is which. Follow a wire from one part. If the only place the current can go next is into a second part, those two are in series. If the two parts share both ends, they are in parallel. Collapse each simple group into a single equivalent value, redraw, and repeat. A tangle of a dozen resistors usually reduces to one number in a few steps. This is the first technique taught in every circuits course, and working engineers never stop using it.
What it does

Proteins are chains of smaller units called amino acids. Your body uses them to build and repair muscle, skin, organs, enzymes, hormones and antibodies. Unlike fat and carbohydrate, protein has no dedicated storage depot. Tissue is constantly being broken down and rebuilt, and the amino acids must be resupplied by food. Of the twenty amino acids the body uses, nine are called essential because it cannot make them. Those must come from what you eat. A diet short of protein for a long period shows up as lost muscle, slow healing and, in children, poor growth.
The official minimum

The recommended dietary allowance in the United States and many other countries is 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. For a person weighing 70 kilograms, that is 56 grams. It is important to understand what this number is. It is the amount estimated to prevent deficiency in nearly all healthy adults. It was not designed as a target for people who are active, building muscle, losing weight or growing older.
When more helps

Research on people doing resistance training points to a higher figure for building muscle. A widely cited analysis of dozens of trials found that the benefit of extra protein levelled off at around 1.6 grams per kilogram per day, with some individuals possibly gaining from a little more. Older adults appear to need more than the minimum to maintain muscle, because ageing muscle responds less strongly to a given dose. People eating less to lose weight also preserve more muscle on a higher intake.
Sources

Animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy contain all nine essential amino acids in useful proportions. Most plant sources are lower in one or more of them, but the gaps differ from food to food, so eating a variety covers them. Beans with rice is the classic pairing. Soy is close to complete on its own. People eating only plants can meet their needs comfortably. They simply need somewhat more total protein and a mix of sources across the day.
Spread it out

The body can only use so much protein for building muscle at one sitting. Many researchers suggest that around 20 to 40 grams per meal, depending on body size, is enough to stimulate that process fully. Typical eating patterns put little protein at breakfast and a great deal at dinner. Shifting some of it earlier in the day is an easy improvement. An egg or two, yoghurt or leftovers from the night before will do it. The total across the day still matters most, so treat the timing as fine tuning.
What 30 grams looks like

It helps to have a few reference points. A chicken breast or a similar piece of fish the size of your palm has about 30 grams. Three eggs have about 18. A cup of Greek yoghurt has roughly 20. A cup of cooked lentils has about 18. A glass of milk has 8. Protein powders are a convenience, not a necessity. They are simply food in concentrated form, and useful mainly when whole foods are impractical.
Sensible limits

For healthy people, intakes well above the minimum have not been shown to harm the kidneys. People with existing kidney disease are a different case and should follow medical advice. Protein also keeps you full for longer than the same calories from carbohydrate or fat, which is one reason higher-protein diets help with weight control. The practical summary is short: include a palm-sized portion of a protein-rich food at each meal, and a little more if you train hard or are past sixty.
The forgetting curve

In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of meaningless syllables and tested himself at intervals. He found that forgetting is steep at first and then levels off. Much of the list was gone within an hour, more within a day, and what survived a few days tended to last. His curve has been reproduced many times since. It explains an experience everyone has had: studying something until it feels solid and finding it mostly gone a week later.
Each review slows the loss

Ebbinghaus also found the remedy. When he relearned a list he had partly forgotten, it took less time than the first learning, and afterwards he forgot it more slowly. Every well-timed review makes the memory more durable, so the gap before the next review can be longer. A fact first reviewed after a day might next be reviewed after three days, then a week, then a month, then several months. A handful of brief reviews can hold something for years.
Spacing beats massing

This is called the spacing effect, and it is among the most reliably demonstrated findings in the study of learning. For the same total study time, sessions spread out over days or weeks produce far better long-term retention than one concentrated session. Cramming does work for an exam the next morning. It simply produces knowledge that evaporates soon after. If you need to know something next year, studying it in one sitting is close to the least efficient method available.
Why difficulty helps

The best moment to review is when recall has become slightly hard but is still possible. That effort of pulling the fact back is what strengthens it. Reviewing too soon feels pleasant and does little, because the answer is still sitting in short-term memory. This is counterintuitive, since easy review feels productive. Psychologists call such obstacles desirable difficulties. Learning that feels smooth is often shallow, and learning that feels like a struggle is often the kind that lasts.
Flashcard systems

In the 1970s the German science writer Sebastian Leitner described a simple system using a row of boxes. New cards start in the first box and are reviewed daily. A card you answer correctly moves to the next box, which is reviewed less often. A card you miss returns to the first. Modern flashcard programs such as Anki automate the same idea, calculating a separate schedule for every card. Medical students and language learners use them to hold tens of thousands of facts.
What it suits

Spaced repetition is built for discrete things you must simply know: vocabulary, anatomy, formulas, dates, legal definitions, the names of people you met. It is less suited to understanding an argument or acquiring a skill, though breaking a subject into good questions often forces understanding along the way. Write cards in your own words, keep each to a single fact, and prefer questions that require recall over ones you can answer by recognition. If you find yourself reciting a whole paragraph to answer a card, it is really several cards and should be split.
A plan without software

You can use the principle with nothing but a calendar. After learning something, review it the next day, then three days later, then after a week, then after a month. Each review can be short, as long as you try to recall before you look. For a course, this means beginning revision in the first week and returning to old material regularly instead of leaving it all for the end. The total time is lower than cramming and the result is knowledge you keep. Language learners who review a little every day routinely outpace those who study for hours once a week.
What inflation is

Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, which is the same thing as a fall in what each unit of money can buy. It is measured by tracking the cost of a broad basket of goods and services. If the basket costs 3 percent more than a year ago, inflation is 3 percent. Individual prices move for their own reasons. Televisions get cheaper while tuition gets dearer. Inflation is the average drift of the whole basket, and your own experience can differ from it depending on what you buy.
How fast money halves

The rule of 72 works here too. Divide 72 by the inflation rate to find how long it takes for money to lose half its buying power. At 2 percent, a rate many central banks aim for, that takes 36 years. At 3 percent, 24 years. At 7 percent, barely 10. A person who retires at 65 on a fixed income and lives to 89 will see their purchasing power roughly halve at 3 percent inflation. Nothing dramatic happens in any one year, which is exactly why it is easy to ignore.
Nominal and real

Economists separate nominal figures, the plain number of dollars, from real figures, adjusted for inflation. If your savings account pays 2 percent and prices rise 3 percent, your nominal return is plus 2 and your real return is about minus 1. You have more dollars and can buy less with them. The same goes for pay. A 3 percent raise in a year of 4 percent inflation is a real pay cut. Thinking in real terms is the single most useful habit for judging any long-term financial number.
Who wins and who loses

Inflation moves wealth around. People holding cash or receiving fixed payments lose, because each payment buys less. Borrowers with fixed-rate debts gain, because they repay with money that is worth less than what they borrowed. A fixed-rate mortgage is the classic example: the payment stays the same while wages and prices generally rise around it. Owners of real things, such as property and businesses, tend to be protected over time, since what they own can be repriced as the general price level climbs.
Why some inflation is intended

Most central banks aim for low, steady inflation, commonly about 2 percent, not zero. Falling prices sound pleasant but can be damaging. If people expect things to be cheaper next year, they delay spending, businesses cut back, and debts become harder to repay because the money owed is growing in value. A small positive rate also gives room for wages and prices to adjust smoothly. High and unpredictable inflation is the damaging kind, because nobody can plan around it.
When it runs away

History holds extreme cases. In Germany in 1923, prices doubled every few days and workers were paid twice daily so they could spend the money before it lost its value. Zimbabwe in 2008 and Hungary in 1946 saw even faster collapses. These episodes share a pattern: a government unable to pay its bills prints money to cover them, and confidence in the currency evaporates. They are rare, but they explain why central banks guard their independence and why the public's expectations matter so much.
What it means for you

Three practical points follow. Money you will not need for many years should be invested in something expected to grow faster than prices, since cash guarantees a slow loss. Long-term goals should be stated in today's dollars and then adjusted, because a million dollars in thirty years will not buy what it buys now. And any promise of a fixed payment far in the future, from a pension to an insurance policy, should be judged by whether it rises with prices or stays flat.
The average result of a decision

Expected value, EV for short, is what a decision earns on average if you could repeat it thousands of times. To find it, multiply each possible outcome by its chance and add them up. Suppose you call 50 dollars to win a pot of 150, and you will win 30 percent of the time. You win 150 three times in ten and lose 50 seven times in ten. That is 45 minus 35, a profit of 10 dollars per call on average. The call is plus EV, even though you lose most of the time.
Good decisions can lose

In the example above you lose the pot seven times out of ten and the call is still correct. A player who judges by results will decide after a few losses that the call was a mistake and stop making it. That player has just made their game worse. The reverse is equally common. Someone calls with a hopeless hand, hits a miracle card and concludes the play works. Short-term results in poker are loud and mostly noise. EV is the quiet signal beneath them.
Every option has an EV

At each decision you are comparing options, not judging one. Folding has an EV of exactly zero from that point: you win nothing and lose nothing more. Money already in the pot is gone and does not count. Calling has some EV. Raising has another. The right play is whichever is highest, and sometimes the best available option is still negative, in which case folding at zero wins. Treating chips already invested as a reason to continue is the sunk cost mistake in its purest form.
Small edges, many times

A single plus EV decision may be worth a dollar or two. That seems trivial until you count how many decisions a regular player makes. Several hundred hands in a live week, tens of thousands a month online. A consistent edge of a fraction of a bet per hand is the whole of a winning player's income. Casinos work the same way with an edge of a few percent on each wager. Nobody gets rich on one hand. They get rich on the same small advantage, repeated without boredom.
The EV of a bluff

A bluff has two outcomes. Either the opponent folds and you win the pot, or they call and you usually lose your bet. Bet 50 into a pot of 100 with nothing. If they fold 40 percent of the time, you win 100 four times in ten and lose 50 six times in ten: 40 minus 30, a profit of 10 dollars. The break-even point for a half-pot bluff is one fold in three. Bluffing is not courage. It is a calculation about how often the other person lets go.
Estimate, do not compute

Nobody runs exact sums at the table. What strong players do is estimate the two or three numbers that matter, then lean the right way. Is this call roughly break-even, clearly good or clearly bad? Will this opponent fold more than a third of the time? Rough answers to the right questions beat precise answers to the wrong ones. The precision comes later, in review, when you can check the hard spots with a calculator and correct your instincts for next time.
Why it protects your mind
